scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Huaconada originates from the village of Mito in the province of Concepción, central Peruvian Andes.
It is a ritual dance with pre-Hispanic roots fused with Spanish colonial elements, symbolizing moral order and social authority.
The dance represents the ancient council of elders who governed the village, now enacted by the huacones during the festival.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Huaconada is performed annually on January 1–3, marking the start of the year.
The huacones embody the village’s highest authority during the festival, enforcing moral order.
The dance symbolizes the traversal of thunder and the power of the condor spirit, linking the community to Andean cosmology and social values.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is led by the tinya, a small indigenous drum that beats out the rhythm for the dance.
An orchestra accompanies the huacones, playing different rhythms.
Listen for the tinya (small indigenous drum).

The music centers on the steady beat of the tinya drum, providing a rhythmic foundation for the huacones' dance steps, accompanied by an orchestra playing varied rhythms that underscore the ritual's solemn and authoritative mood.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Elder huacones wear traditional attire including wool hats or chuco, serge garments such as a white cape (blanchet), black pants, white apron, wool socks, and rustic leather sandals called llanques.
Their wooden masks have grotesque features with prominent noses shaped like a condor's beak.
Younger huacones wear colorful modern costumes and masks expressing emotions like terror or sadness.

scenes.title: A respectful note
